extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy and aesthetics, especially those interested in music, tragedy, and the theory of art
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Schopenhauer's aesthetic criteria for tragedy and music: how tragedy should present misfortune and how music functions as a direct objectification of the will (its expressive means, roles of melody/harmony/bass, relation to words, and what kinds of musical imitation are legitimate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential nature of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of a great misfortune is alone essential to tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy must present a great misfortune; peripheral matters aside, its core is the powerful depiction of suffering that leads to profound insight or resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of introducing tragic misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may introduce the great misfortune by (1) a character of extraordinary wickedness, (2) blind fate i.e., chance and error, or (3) the mere position and relations of the dramatis personæ forcing ordinary characters to injure one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer lists examples for each: (1) Richard III., Iago, Shylock; (2) Œdipus Rex, many ancient tragedies, Romeo and Juliet; (3) Clavigo, parts of Hamlet, Wallenstein, Faust (Gretchen episode). He judges the third kind superior because it brings misfortune near and everyday.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of relational/situational tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy arising from the relations and positions of ordinary characters surpasses tragedies based on monstrous wickedness or prodigious fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kind shows misfortune as arising easily from typical human actions and relations, making it terrible and immediate; it is also the most difficult to achieve because the greatest effect must be produced with minimal, believable causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's moral object: original sin and renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: True tragedy reveals that the hero atones not for particular individual sins but for original sin — the crime of existence itself — often culminating in renunciation of life or the will to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great tragic figures, purified by suffering, renounce life or their former ends; examples include characters from Calderon, Goethe’s Gretchen, Hamlet, Joan of Arc. The tragic effect is the hero's insight and surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'poetical justice' as a requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for poetical justice misunderstands the nature of tragedy and of the world; absence of poetic justice does not invalidate tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism demanding that crimes be visibly punished (e.g., Samuel Johnson on Shakespeare) mistakes the point; tragic power often lies in injustice that is not morally tidy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's ontological uniqueness among the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Music stands alone, cut off from other arts: unlike them it does not represent the Ideas (phenomena) but is the direct copy or objectification of the will itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music is not a copy of the phenomenal world but a more direct expression of the in-itself; its effect is stronger, quicker, more necessary and infallible than other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music expresses universals, not particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Music does not express particular definite joys, sorrows, or events, but joy, sorrow, pain, horror, delight, merriment, peace_of_mind themselves — the quintessence or universals of feeling, abstracted from motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because music gives the inmost kernel (the 'thing-in-itself') rather than the external phenomenon, it can be set to many different texts or examples; text must remain subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against close union of words and music in opera
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of opera should never make itself the chief thing and the music a mere means of expressing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When music becomes too closely united to words and tries to form itself according to events, it speaks a language not its own. Rossini is praised for keeping music free so it can 'speak its own language'; songs and operas work best when music retains its universality and the text remains subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of specially imitative (program) music
rubrics_metrics.description: Music that directly imitates external phenomena (program music: e.g., 'The Seasons' by Haydn, some passages of 'Creation', battle-pieces) is to be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such music merely imitates phenomena and thereby gives an inadequate imitation of the will's phenomena instead of expressing the will itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy of musical registers to grades of objectification of will
rubrics_metrics.description: The deep bass corresponds to unorganised nature (the crudest mass); complemental parts correspond to lower grades (plants and beasts); the high singing melody corresponds to the intellectual life and effort of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low tones (bass) move slowly and represent the origin, higher parts move quicker without the connecting development of melody, while melody alone has unbroken significant connection representing human intellect; composers can exploit these correspondences expressively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody as the record of the intellectually enlightened will
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody, the high singing principal voice with unbroken intentional connection, records the history and inner movements of the intellectually enlightened will — every excitement, effort, and feeling not capturable by abstract concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melodic structure should show significant intentional progression from beginning to end, reflecting reasoned continuity of human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of melodic features to human willing (tempo, mode, deviations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick transitions and short intelligible subjects (dance-music) express cheerful, easily attained pleasure; slow melodies, striking painful discords and long returns to the keynote express sadness and delayed satisfaction (ennui); Allegro maestoso signifies noble effort; Adagio expresses painful effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositional choices of tempo, length, and deviation should map to the quality of will-striving being expressed (e.g., minor mode extends pain; major relieves it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive use of minor and major modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of half a tone — minor third instead of major — at once produces an anxious, painful feeling, and the major immediately delivers us from it; Adagio in minor becomes a convulsive wail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ minor/major contrasts deliberately: minor for sustained pain or failure, major for release and relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional origin: inspiration over conscious concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of melody is the work of genius and inspiration, which lies far from reflection and conscious intention; in the composer the man is separated from the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine musical expression arises from immediate inspiration, not from deliberate conceptual imitation; the concept is 'unfruitful' in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of full harmonic context for musical expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Music achieves its full effect only in complete harmony: the high leading voice (melody) requires the accompaniment of all other voices down to the lowest bass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melody and harmony enter into each other; full union of voices parallels the full objectification of will in the world. Solo melody without harmonic context is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's formal constraints and the inevitability of temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly accurate, pure system of tones is arithmetically impossible; all possible music deviates from perfect purity and must conceal essential discords by temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperament and measured impurity are not flaws but necessities of the musical system; composers and theorists must acknowledge and work within this arithmetical constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music perceived temporally, apart from space and causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is perceived in and through time alone, with absolute exclusion of space and apart from the influence of the knowledge of causality; tones make the aesthetic impression as effect without referring to their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temporal-only perception gives music its unique aesthetic status and immediacy; composers exploit temporal unfolding rather than spatial arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and Da capo appropriate in music
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitions and Da capo, which would be unbearable in verbal language, are appropriate and beneficial in music because to comprehend music fully we must hear it more than once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of repetition is a legitimate and often necessary musical device to deepen comprehension and aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's function: render the visibility of the will more distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: If the visible world is the objectification of the will, then the work of art renders this visibility more distinct and concentrated; the artist attains deep knowledge of the inner nature of the world but bears the suffering of willing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works of art by how clearly and purely they make the idea (objectified will) visible — the work of art is the 'camera obscura' that clarifies perception of the world-as-idea.
